deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is Hilbert's research notebook (Cod. Ms. Hilbert 600). The page is a programmatic note, not a computation, on the uniformization of algebraic curves by automorphic functions.

(a) Thesis. The right foundation for the theory of algebraic functions is Poincaré's (Fuchsian) automorphic functions. The reason given is that a compact Riemann surface X of genus p appears transparently as a circular-arc polygon. In modern terms X = H/Γ, with Γ a Fuchsian group and fundamental domain a hyperbolic 4p-gon with side pairings. The correct number of moduli also appears directly. [My filling-in:] Γ has 2p hyperbolic generators in PSL(2,R), each with 3 real parameters, giving 6p. Subtract 3 for the relation Π[a_i,b_i]=1 and 3 for conjugation. This leaves 6p−6 real = 3p−3 complex parameters, matching Riemann's count of moduli for p≥2. By Gauss–Bonnet, the 4p-gon (vertices forming one cycle, angle sum 2π) has area (4p−2)π − 2π = 4π(p−1).

(b) Existence must be proved differently from Poincaré. Hilbert proposes two routes.

Route 1 (exhaustion / successive continuation). Cut X along a canonical system of cuts into a simply connected surface X_0 ('eindeutig gemacht'). Map X_0 conformally onto the half-plane. Across the cut edges, attach further copies of the surface, overlapping one another and arranged like a wreath ('kranzförmig') around the original, and map each enlarged surface onto the half-plane. Then show the sequence converges, i.e. that one reaches a limit. In modern terms: exhaust the universal cover by increasing simply connected pieces, uniformize each by the Riemann mapping theorem, and pass to the limit. This yields the universal covering map H → X. Hilbert asks in parentheses whether this is 'Schlesinger's method'.

Route 2 (continuity method). Work in a space whose dimension equals the number of moduli (3p−3). Map the totality M_p of Riemann surfaces of genus p onto the totality of Poincaré circular-arc polygons, i.e. Fuchsian groups up to conjugation, and show by a continuity argument that the map is bijective.

To give M_p a concrete definition, Hilbert takes the Noether–Weber–Klein normal curve. This is the canonical curve φ: X → P^{p−1}, given by a basis (φ_1..φ_p) of holomorphic differentials, of degree 2p−2. Its 'boundary' (the degenerations at the boundary of the parameter region) is to be found using Noether's quadratic relations. These are the linear relations Σ c_ij φ_iφ_j = 0 among products of differentials, of which there are p(p+1)/2 − (3p−3) = (p−2)(p−3)/2. This boundary must correspond to the boundary of the polygon space. The sentence continues on the next page: the polygon boundary is found from the conditions that opposite arcs of the Poincaré polygon are carried into each other.
errors: No computational errors; the page is a research plan. Two implicit gaps should be noted.
The canonical map is an embedding only for non-hyperelliptic curves. The hyperelliptic locus needs separate treatment, and Hilbert does not mention it.

Noether's quadrics cut out the canonical curve only if it is neither trigonal nor a plane quintic (Petri 1923). So 'defining the totality via Noether's quadratic relations' needs more care than stated.

The continuity method requires a topological invariance-of-domain argument and properness at the boundary. These were the well-known gaps in the Klein–Poincaré method, closed only by Brouwer and Koebe around 1912. The plan identifies the boundary issue but does not resolve it.
Route 1's convergence ('dass man zu einer Grenze kommt') is the entire difficulty. It was only achieved rigorously in 1907 by Koebe and Poincaré, using Harnack/Koebe distortion-type estimates.

results.what: Representation of a genus-p Riemann surface as a quotient of the half-plane by a Fuchsian group, with a 4p-sided circular-arc fundamental polygon, and the modulus count 3p−3
results.modern_name: Uniformization of compact Riemann surfaces of genus ≥2 by Fuchsian groups; Teichmüller/Fricke moduli count
results.usually_credited_to: Klein and Poincaré (1881–84); rigorous proofs by Koebe and Poincaré (1907)

results.what: Existence via successive conformal mapping of an exhausting sequence of pieces of the universal cover, passing to a limit
results.modern_name: Exhaustion proof of the uniformization theorem (universal covering via Riemann mapping and a limit)
results.usually_credited_to: Koebe 1907, Poincaré 1907 (precursors: Schwarz, Schottky; Hilbert queries Schlesinger)

results.what: Existence via a continuity method between the space of moduli (described by canonical curves) and the space of Fuchsian polygons, matching boundaries
results.modern_name: Klein–Poincaré continuity method (Kontinuitätsmethode); Fricke–Teichmüller space vs moduli space
results.usually_credited_to: Klein, Poincaré (1882–84); made rigorous by Brouwer and Koebe (1911–12)

results.what: Using the canonical (Noether–Weber–Klein normal) curve in P^{p−1} and Noether's quadratic relations among products of differentials to parametrize all Riemann surfaces of genus p
results.modern_name: Canonical embedding and Max Noether's theorem; Petri's theorem on quadrics through the canonical curve

deep.surprise_reason: Hilbert's interest in rigorous uniformization is well known: his 22nd problem (1900) explicitly mentions Poincaré's continuity method and its difficulties. This page shows him earlier sketching both the exhaustion approach and a continuity approach based on the canonical curve. That is a nice pre-1900 glimpse but contains no new result.

checkable.asserts: Fuchsian group parameter count: 2p generators × 3 real parameters, minus 3 for the relation, minus 3 for conjugation, gives 6p−6 real = 3p−3 complex moduli
Gauss–Bonnet: area of a hyperbolic 4p-gon with angle sum 2π equals 4π(p−1)
Number of independent Noether quadratic relations among products of the p holomorphic differentials is (p−2)(p−3)/2
Degree of the canonical curve in P^{p−1} equals 2p−2
